narrative:
The model estimates a 46% chance that you will leave your job, which is high enough for the company to deny your promotion as a precaution.

Three main factors shaped this outlook. First, your total years of experience across all jobs had the strongest influence and pulled the prediction toward staying. At 1-5 years you sit in the most common group among employees the model expects to remain, yet the pattern in the data still suggests this early-career stage often signals higher mobility.

Second, having received other job offers while at the company was the next strongest driver and pushed the prediction toward leaving. This factor indicates you have external opportunities that many employees who stay simply do not possess.

Third, working in the “other” sector also nudged the outcome toward leaving. Only 21.7% of employees the model predicts will stay work in this category, compared with higher shares in medical and education fields.

Taken together, your broad experience and external opportunities outweigh the stabilising effect of your shorter tenure, leading the model to see elevated turnover risk. The company should discuss your career goals openly with you and explore whether targeted support, clearer growth paths, or retention incentives could shift the outlook. You, in turn, may want to reflect on whether the opportunities you have received align with your long-term plans here.
